summary.text:
A council that has been doing exactly what the last two years rewarded, and says so plainly. External borrowing closed at £236m after early repayment of some debt saved £4.5m and smoothed the maturity profile. Treasury investments fell £114m to £171m, described in the report itself as 'a deliberate strategy to borrow internally instead of borrowing externally, which is more efficient'. Investment income of £11.4m against a £4.7m budget is flagged, rightly, as windfall rather than run-rate.

The pressure is on the cash side. Funding the cumulative SEND deficit is what has drawn balances down, and while a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the historic DSG overspend is expected in autumn 2026, two further years of accruing deficits are expected behind it and the Statutory Override does not lapse until March 2028. Internal borrowing only works while the cash lasts.

The covering report carries no CFR — the prudential indicators sit in Appendix 1, which we have not read — so no internal-borrowing figure is recorded here. What we can say is that our holding of their PWLB loans at 31 March comes to £236.2m across 41 loans, against the £236m of total borrowing in the report. Four officer addresses are published, which is the most of any council in either batch.

officer.subject: The £4.5m you saved, and what moves it
officer.body:
Hi Chris,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts ahead of Audit and Standards on 17 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your outturn report does something most don't, which is label the £11.4m of investment income as windfall rather than run-rate. That's the sentence a committee needs and it's usually missing.

A cross-check first: our holding of your PWLB loans at 31 March comes to £236.2m across 41 loans, against the £236m of total borrowing in your highlights.

The line that caught us is the £4.5m saved on early repayment, and that it bought a smoother maturity profile as well as cash. That's the same arithmetic we run daily — every council's book priced against the DMO's premature repayment curve, premium or discount, at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. It moves more than people expect: one council we read this month saw its net discount position swing £6.6m in a single quarter. Whether anything has moved back into range since March is a page rather than a piece of work, and we'd never present it as a quote — the DMO's is the binding one.

The other half of the picture is that the strategy behind all this has a cash constraint attached, and your report says so. Investments fell £114m to £171m because you've been borrowing internally instead of externally, which was plainly the right call while investment returns sat under borrowing costs. But the drawdown is being driven by the cumulative SEND deficit, and while the High Needs Stability Grant should cover 90% of the historic overspend in the autumn, two more years of accruing deficits sit behind it and the Statutory Override runs to March 2028. Internal borrowing is cheap right up until the cash runs out.

Where that lands depends on the curve on the day you need it. Ten-year certainty money is 5.83% today and twenty-year 6.38%, both a little above where they sat at the end of March, and Bank Rate — 3.75% — is currently priced to rise to about 4.11% within a year rather than fall. The rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds, both fixings, whole curve. The monthly sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is the other half: July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%, so you can see how much appetite there is before you need it rather than after.

On training, three fit Warwickshire: Break costs and premature repayment, given the £4.5m you've just banked; Cost of carry and internal borrowing, for the strategy your report describes; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — it's the indicator that tells you when the internal position stops being the cheaper option, and worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee this goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
